entities.name: The Tale of Genji (Genji Monogatari)
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Written by the court lady Murasaki Shikibu (c. 973–c. 1014/1025 CE) in the early 11th century, The Tale of Genji is widely considered the world's first psychological novel and the supreme masterpiece of Japanese literature. In 54 chapters spanning three generations, it follows the life, loves, and political fortunes of Hikaru Genji ("the Shining Prince"), an illegitimate son of an ancient Japanese emperor, and his descendants.

The novel's extraordinary psychological depth — its nuanced portrayal of human desire, jealousy, longing, aging, and loss — anticipates by 800 years the concerns of the modern European novel. Its pervasive aesthetic of mono no aware ("the pathos of things" — a bittersweet awareness of impermanence) became a defining concept of Japanese culture. Written entirely in the Japanese kana syllabary (rather than Chinese), it established the legitimacy of Japanese as a literary language.
